reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The most concrete measured figure for this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Other services, the NAICS 81 grouping that includes grantmaking and civic organizations, the latest reading is 12.7%, down from a prior period of 15.0%. That is the only hard adoption number in the material, and it describes a broad services category rather than nonprofits alone, so it should be read as an adjacent signal rather than a nonprofit-specific rate. The Census Bureau page itself supplies no further detail beyond confirming the survey exists.

On what AI is actually used for, the Center for Effective Philanthropy is the source that speaks most directly. Its sector research, including AI-focused reporting, examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. CEP's own material describes assessments that gather feedback from grantees, donors, and funder staff, benchmarking grantmakers against each other, and a fourth annual State of Nonprofits report on how nonprofits are faring amid what it calls unprecedented challenges. CEP also frames the moment as one in which operating on a high moral and ethical plane while keeping a brand strong has become increasingly complicated but also more important. That is the sector's characteristic tension in the sources: adoption questions are entangled with trust and reputation questions.

The Nonprofit Technology Network approaches the same territory from the technology-investment side. NTEN runs regular sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits, and its page states plainly that nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and the sector that must be dismantled. It promotes an Equity Guide pledge and celebrates open source tools built for nonprofit and advocacy use. The AI Equity Project covers similar ground from the access angle, describing structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, work that turns public libraries and community spaces into learning environments pairing senior citizens with student volunteers, and a global network providing standardized technical curricula to underrepresented communities. Neither organization's harvested text reports a deployment rate or an ROI figure, so the material supports describing the access and equity agenda but not quantifying it.

On money and where it concentrates, Candid is the source named for the funding side. It describes itself as providing grants and nonprofit data to help find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders, and the sourced point credits it with tracking grantmaking trends including funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure. The World of AI's own ecosystem page adds a narrow but auditable data point: four individually verified organizations appear under Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations touching AI tooling and evaluation. It names LMSYS, which stewards Chatbot Arena as shared evaluation infrastructure outside the commercial incentives of the labs being evaluated, Khan Academy as an end-user of AI in education rather than a producer, and the Krita and Blender foundations as creative software stewards whose missions predate AI. The same page is explicit about what it does not cover: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, no open-model foundations releasing weights, and no funding scale, compute access, or governance detail. That silence is itself informative for anyone looking for infrastructure-level nonprofit AI activity.

Stanford HAI supplies the macro frame rather than sector numbers. Its AI Index describes a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating, and adoption spreading while governance, evaluation, and understanding frameworks fall behind, and it notes declining data transparency. HAI also states that AI's benefits will not be evenly distributed unless development is guided thoughtfully, and it relies on philanthropic support for its own work. For a nonprofit reader, that is the governance-capacity constraint stated at the highest level of generality the sources offer.

What a reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this is limited but real. The Census Bureau gives one measured adoption figure for an adjacent services category, 12.7% latest against 15.0% prior, and nothing in the material explains the movement. CEP and NTEN describe how the sector studies and supports AI use, with CEP emphasizing ethics and brand and NTEN emphasizing equity and digital maturity. Candid covers the funding pipeline, the AI Equity Project covers the training and access gap, and The World of AI's catalogue shows a small verified population of nonprofit and open-source AI organizations with no infrastructure players among them. No source here reports a nonprofit-specific ROI figure, and none reports a nonprofit-specific regulatory posture, so those questions remain open on this evidence.

https://cep.org/.brief: CEP describes itself as working to make foundations and major donors more effective, offering assessments that collect feedback from grantees, donors and funder staff and benchmark results against other grantmakers, alongside research, advisory services, events and blog commentary. The page promotes a limited-time discount of up to $1000 for signing up before Oct. 30 for a 2027 assessment or custom advisory project. It highlights CEP's fourth annual State of Nonprofits report, which it says offers insight into how nonprofits are faring amid unprecedented challenges, and references a webinar on its research titled "Evolving Foundation Responses to a Sector in Crisis." The page also includes a piece by Carmen Rojas, identified as president and CEO of the Marguerite Casey Foundation, on endowment investment as part of stewardship, and a note that a form requires JavaScript.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid describes itself as a provider of grants and nonprofit data intended to help people find funding, research nonprofits and connect with funders. It says analysts, advocates and philanthropists use its information to build a broad picture of social sector activity, and it invites readers to learn how it collects, organises and distributes that data. The page also flags several topics it covers: the conditions attached to most grant funding and some donations, and the strain those conditions place on nonprofits; one foundation's stated reasons for sharing its grantmaking data with Candid, which it frames as a matter of transparency; and the argument that recognition, media coverage, partnerships and growth do not by themselves make a nonprofit financially sustainable, since it needs ongoing unrestricted support. It notes that impact evaluations are growing in importance for nonprofits and funders alike, and offers an email list for insights, trends, product updates and research.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index.brief: The AI Index at Stanford HAI describes its mission as supplying unbiased, globally sourced data on artificial intelligence for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public, tracking and visualising data on the field. This year's edition, the page says, shows a widening gap between what AI can do and our readiness to manage it, with technical capabilities, investment and adoption advancing while governance and evaluation frameworks lag. The page states that previous editions have been cited in newspapers including The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, drawn hundreds of academic citations, and been referenced by policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It describes the programme as an independent Stanford HAI initiative led by an interdisciplinary steering committee, and notes a collaboration with Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez on regulatory frameworks.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues four individually verified organisations classified as nonprofits or open-source foundations, each with a sourced note and the date that source was last read. It states that LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform used by the wider AI community to benchmark model quality, while Khan Academy is described as an end-user rather than a producer of AI capability. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation are said to steward creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, though their missions predate AI. The page notes that it contains no training compute providers, no standards bodies for grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights, and that its notes confirm only organisational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.
